overview: This record follows Māori communities in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Gardens, crafts and ancestral taonga reveal knowledge rooted in particular places. Iwi and hapū had distinct histories and authority, not a single state.

periods.title: Gardens and local knowledge
periods.summary: Stonefield gardens at Ihumātao and modified soils in Waikato show sustained work to cultivate crops in local conditions. Their development was regional and gradual. This broad phase does not assign all surviving structures to one construction date.

sections.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape

items.text: Ōtuataua Stonefields at Ihumātao preserve rows, heaps and mounds associated with cultivation on volcanic ground. The specialised system may have developed by the fifteenth or sixteenth century. Adding sand and gravel and arranging stone helped growers manage soil and growing conditions.

Shell middens at Ōtuataua, including deposits dated to the sixteenth or seventeenth century, show that coastal foods accompanied gardening. Habitation areas and storage features place food production within a lived landscape rather than an isolated agricultural installation.

Today’s stonefields contain features from different periods. Māori gardens, house sites, cooking shelters and terraces share the landscape with nineteenth-century European drystone walls. A visible wall is therefore not automatically evidence of a pre-contact Māori garden boundary.

sections.title: Gardening and the work of clothing

items.text: In the middle Waikato Basin, modified soils and borrow pits record intensive horticulture from the sixteenth century. Gardeners moved gravel into cultivation areas. Storage pits and planting features add evidence of sustained labour in managing root crops.

Whatu forms cloth by twining horizontal threads around vertical ones with the fingers. Muka fibre extracted from harakeke supplied material for cloaks. Raranga uses plaiting, commonly for mats and baskets. These related crafts solve different structural problems.

Rain capes combine a worked foundation with overlapping plant strips that shed water. Scraped sections allowed the strips to be attached as the garment grew. The construction joined knowledge of fibre preparation, fastening and weather protection; no exact invention date is established here.

Te Papa presents weaving’s whakapapa through Hine-te-iwaiwa, guardian of weaving, childbirth and lunar cycles. In this tradition, women transmit the skills and knowledge. Craft is understood through relationships among people, ancestors and the natural world as well as through technique.

Uenuku, an ancestral carving held at Te Awamutu Museum, represents an atua of Tainui. Tainui tradition associates the spirit of Uenuku with the voyaging waka. The museum gives a broad traditional dating range; this card does not convert it into a precise manufacture year.

For many iwi, Matariki’s return to the winter dawn sky marks a new year. Remembrance, harvest thanksgiving and sharing food connect observation of the heavens with community life. Timing and observance vary among iwi; there was no single uniform national calendar.

ending.text: Māori communities continue beyond this map interval. Ōtuataua retains local ancestral connections. Later colonial confiscation caused dispossession, while iwi and hapū persisted. Kōhanga reo supports continuing cultural transmission.
